name: Leading geographic dateline
instruction: Mark headlines that begin with “In” followed by a place, or with a country or city name. This can reveal foreign-desk or bureau-origin conventions.

name: Practical service promise
instruction: High when the headline promises advice, instructions, or help with a decision; low when it offers no usable guidance; it does not apply without a service frame

name: Mystery-death hook
instruction: Score high when an unexplained death or unexplained cause is the core hook ('something in room', serial killings, radiation spike). Score low when cause of harm is stated.

name: Ideological Polarization
instruction: Scores high when opposing political, religious, national, or moral camps are identifiable; low when disagreement is technical or no stance is present. It does not apply when group positions are not explicit.

name: Location-heavy wording
instruction: named geography | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing two or more explicit countries, cities, regions, or national demonyms.

name: Celebrity personal-name slot
instruction: Headline leads with a bare celebrity name plus colon (Harry:, Matthew Perry:, KSI, Malala), reflecting entertainment desk conventions and promoted sidebar placement.

name: Social-Identity Resonance
instruction: Scores high when the headline invokes a shared group identity, belonging, or identity-related value; low when no group identity is implicated. It does not apply when relevance requires personal details absent from the headline.

name: Withholds exactly the detail the headline makes the reader want
instruction: Score 0-10 for whether the headline sets up a specific, legitimate question in the reader's mind whose answer is in the story -- who, how much, what happened next -- without being deceptive about what the story contains. 10 = a precise curiosity gap a reader can only close by reading; 0 = either everything is already in the headline or the gap is vague clickbait that the story cannot pay off.

name: Domestic-UK angle tell
instruction: Explicit mention of UK, England, or a UK institution (NHS, PM), flagging the home-audience desk whose readership baseline is higher.

name: Quoted speech
instruction: Mark headlines containing quotation marks around a phrase or sentence. Quoted headlines may fingerprint interview, reaction, or live-news formats.

name: Concrete Scene Vividness
instruction: Scores high when the headline depicts a specific sensory scene, object, or action that is readily pictured; low when wording is abstract or bureaucratic. It does not apply when no concrete scene is conveyed.

name: In-quote ordinary voice
instruction: Quoted first-person speech from a non-public figure ("I cut a carrot...", "'litres and litres'") marks magazine/features commissions.

name: Numerical specificity
instruction: Mark digits, percentages, ages, counts, or precise quantities. This may fingerprint data-led, health, or breaking-news treatments.

name: First-person voice
instruction: Score high when the headline contains a first-person pronoun or quoted speech ('I', 'we', 'our', 'litres and litres'). Score low when it is entirely third-person institutional reporting.

name: Source Transparency
instruction: Scores high when the headline identifies a source, evidence, or attribution that clarifies claim provenance; low when it presents an unsupported assertion. It does not apply to plainly observable events without contested claims.

name: Follow-up headline ellipticalness
instruction: Headline omits full names/events and relies on assumed prior knowledge ("Why Donald Trump lost", "The biggest news wasn't about Manafort"), signalling day 2+ of a running story.

name: Running-story recap framing
instruction: Mark “what do we know,” “explaining,” “why …,” “latest images,” or similar recap language. Such wording may fingerprint a later position in a multi-day story or a designated explainer slot.

name: Explicit question-mark headline
instruction: Headline ends in a question mark, e.g. "What do we know?" or "Did...start in...?"

name: Explicit emotion word
instruction: Headline contains emotion terms (fear, outrage, love, demons, gross). Scores high when emotion is the story; not for neutral reporting

name: Signals direct consequence for the reader's own life
instruction: Score 0-10 for whether the headline makes clear that the story affects the reader personally -- their money, health, commute, bills, weather, rights -- and roughly how. 10 = the personal stake is explicit and concrete; 0 = no implication that the reader's own circumstances are touched.

name: Explanation or analysis marker
instruction: Score high when the headline signals explainer or analytical framing ('Why...', 'Explaining...', 'The rise and fall'). Score low for breaking-event headlines.

name: Curiosity gap
instruction: Score high when the headline withholds key information the reader must click to resolve ('this photo', 'wasn't about Manafort', 'something in room'). Score low when the headline states its own conclusion.

name: Personal welfare stakes
instruction: High when it signals direct effects on people’s health, safety, rights, or daily routines; low when consequences remain remote or institutional; it does not apply without individual consequences

name: Contains the word 'you' or 'your'
instruction: Score 0-10 for occurrences of the literal tokens 'you', 'your' or 'yours' in the headline. 10 = several occurrences or one in the opening two words; 0 = none. Count the tokens only; do not judge whether the story actually concerns the reader.

name: Headline word count
instruction: Score 0-10 for how long the headline is in words. 10 = very long (13+ words); 5 = around 8-9 words; 0 = 4 words or fewer. Judge extent only -- do not consider whether the length serves the story.

name: Scare-quoted scepticism marker
instruction: Single quoted word casting doubt ('deceptive', 'unidentified', 'no value'). Scores low-to-moderate; hedge weakens urgency

name: POLARIZATION
instruction: Scores high when the headline presents opposing camps or a divisive proposition; low when it describes consensus or a technical matter. It does not apply when disagreement is not explicitly stated

name: Mundane-relatable action
instruction: Score high when the headline centres on an everyday, ordinary activity framed as remarkable (cutting a carrot, losing a teddy bear). Score low when actions are institutional or geopolitical.

name: Reader-addressing question
instruction: Headline is phrased as a question to the reader ("What do we know?", "How will we know...?"). Scores high; does not apply to reported questions
